title: 6 times drivers improvised after losing radio during a race
excerpt:
Max Verstappen might have sealed a dominant victory at the Singapore Grand Prix last weekend, but his race was not entirely without hiccups – the four-time World Champion having suffered issues with his radio during the event.

While Verstappen could hear his Race Engineer Gianpiero Lambiase, the Dutchman’s responses were inaudible – leading to some creative solutions from Lambiase, who developed a code of sorts by asking yes/no questions where Verstappen either had to stay silent or respond with a button press. The Red Bull team also made use of pit boards to communicate with their driver.

Verstappen is not the only driver to experience this kind of problem during a race, with several other well-known names facing radio glitches in the past – sometimes with very interesting consequences…

Sebastian Vettel and Mark Webber, 2012 Malaysian Grand Prix

While only one of Red Bull’s cars appeared to be suffering radio issues at Marina Bay in 2026, the team have previously seen this affect both sides of the garage – as was the case in the rain-affected 2012 Malaysian Grand Prix.

After the race was suspended due to heavy downpours, it soon became apparent when the action resumed that Sebastian Vettel and Mark Webber were experiencing communications problems. Initially this did not seem to be hampering Vettel too much, who was running in fourth while relying on the pit board.

However, after a late-race collision with Narain Karthikeyan while lapping the HRT, the team tried to call Vettel in for safety reasons – only for him not to hear the message. The German still managed to get his car over the line in P11, but conceded that losing radio had made the Grand Prix “very difficult”.

As for Webber, a fourth-place finish was a solid result on such a tough day yet it was not without its frustrations, the Australian admitting that he had resorted to tearing the radio out of his helmet due to the loud static becoming a distraction in already challenging conditions.

Michael Schumacher, 1999 French Grand Prix

Michael Schumacher made a number of memorable overtakes during his hugely successful F1 career – but it was some moves of a different kind from the German that caught the eye when disaster struck at the French Grand Prix in 1999.

In a rain-hit encounter at the Magny-Cours Circuit, Schumacher was looking to add further points to his tally as he battled reigning champion Mika Hakkinen for the title. That goal hit a snag, though, when the Ferrari lost communication with the pit wall.

Some quick-thinking from Schumacher resulted in a resolution of sorts, however, as the then-two time World Champion started to use hand signals towards his onboard camera to communicate with the team – given that he could be seen but not heard.

While this could not prevent him from ultimately ending the race back in fifth following a slow pit stop, it was certainly a noteworthy response to the radio problems.

Alex Albon, 2025 Las Vegas Grand Prix

For many drivers, losing communication during a race can be a hugely frustrating – and potentially result-affecting – occurrence. However, it seems that there can be some silver linings...

Alex Albon spent much of the 2025 Las Vegas Grand Prix without functioning radio after losing connection on his laps to the grid, leading him to quip afterwards that it was “pretty peaceful out there”.

On a more serious note, though, the Williams driver admitted that this had left him in the dark about how much damage he might be carrying following an incident at the start of the race, with communication limited to the pit boards.

Albon ultimately retired from the event rather than risk continuing due to the threat of safety issues, highlighting just how vital radio messages can be during a Grand Prix.

Max Verstappen, 2021 French Grand Prix

Verstappen’s success in Singapore despite his communication difficulties was impressive – and it appears to be an area that the Dutchman has form in.

Back in 2021, Verstappen was locked in a famously tense title fight with Lewis Hamilton and the Mercedes team. The Red Bull man held the lead in the standings when the paddock headed to Paul Ricard for the seventh round of the campaign, the French Grand Prix.

A two-stop strategy helped Verstappen to overtake Hamilton for the lead with just two laps remaining, giving the former his third victory of the season – despite the fact that, like in Singapore, a radio problem in the latter stages meant that he could receive his team’s messages but they could not hear him.

While Lambiase had advised him to try moving the microphone when convenient, the gremlins remained until the chequered flag – but the Dutch driver later played down the impact of the issue, given that it had only occurred after he had completed his pit stops.

Charles Leclerc, 2023 Hungarian Grand Prix

Although some drivers appear to take radio glitches in their stride, the problem is undoubtedly difficult and can lead to frustrations boiling over – particularly when coupled with other issues, as Charles Leclerc discovered at the Hungarian Grand Prix in 2023.

It was not the Monegasque’s day at the Hungaroring, where he experienced everything from his drinks tube being too short – meaning that he had no water during the race – through to a slow pit stop and then a five-second time penalty for speeding in the pit lane.

On top of this, Leclerc – who ended the event in P7 – suggested later on that struggles with the radio had been one of his key gripes during the race, explaining: “One out of four words is not understood by my engineer, because there's just problems with our radios in three, four races.

“So we need to fix that. And obviously my tone of voice is quite high because I need to make myself heard.”

Lewis Hamilton and Valtteri Bottas, 2017 Hungarian Grand Prix

As mentioned earlier, Red Bull know what it is like for both cars to lose transmission – and the same can be said for Mercedes, whose radio issues came at a crucial time in their fight for both titles back in 2017.

While the Ferraris of Sebastian Vettel – who led the championship by one point from Hamilton at that stage – and Kimi Raikkonen held first and second positions during the Hungarian Grand Prix, Valtteri Bottas was running in third ahead of team mate Hamilton.

The decision was made to invert the cars in order for Hamilton – who looked to have more pace – to attempt to chase after the Scuderia machines. However, radio issues were affecting both Silver Arrows cars, with Team Principal Toto Wolff later explaining that “our whole comms and data systems broke down” due to a crack in a fibre optic cable, leaving the squad to “fly blind”.

These problems particularly affected Hamilton and, while the Briton did overtake Bottas, he later honoured the plan to hand the position back if he was unable to pass Raikkonen. Hamilton conceded afterwards, though, that the swap could have been carried out sooner had it not been for the radio struggles.

This all resulted in Hamilton’s deficit to Vettel extending to 14 points, causing some concern for Mercedes at the time – but as we now know, a successful run for the British driver in the second half would see him clinch his fourth World Championship.

title: How the pecking order has changed since the season opener
excerpt:
The pecking order was always expected to shift under the new-for-2026 regulations, but as teams have fought to adapt to those changes by introducing upgrades, it’s shuffled around even more.

Mercedes looked unstoppable at the start of the season, and while Kimi Antonelli still has a commanding lead in the Drivers’ Championship, the competition has closed in around him to the stage where we’ve seen race winners from three other teams.

Nevertheless, the Silver Arrows remain the benchmark – you’d be bold to say otherwise considering their 134-point advantage over Ferrari – so we’ve crunched the numbers to assess just how much their rivals have improved.

From Red Bull’s admirable turnaround to the near-complete overhaul of Aston Martin’s challenger, let’s dive into the data…

Qualifying pace

Mercedes have claimed 11 of the 17 Grand Prix pole positions so far, with Antonelli taking six of those – just one up on his team mate George Russell. As such, they were determined to be the fastest on ultimate Qualifying pace (i.e. their ideal lap if they were to put their best sectors together) in 13 rounds.

That was the case even when they were beaten to the top spot, like when Lando Norris qualified P1 in the Netherlands. They’ve actually dropped down the order in recent events, which saw Max Verstappen build the biggest advantage over Mercedes than at any point so far this season through his pole lap in Malaysia – where Antonelli and Russell could only manage P4 and P8 respectively.

Red Bull have enjoyed one of the greatest improvements, going from the low of a >1% gap to Mercedes in Japan to beating not only the Constructors’ Championship leaders, but also Ferrari and McLaren in Round 16.

Speaking of the Scuderia, their ultimate pace reveals that they’ve missed some opportunities for better results in Qualifying. In Singapore, for instance, Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc had almost 0.2s on the rest of the field, so could’ve dominated had they added up their fastest sectors.

However, they struggled to put it all together and Verstappen subsequently qualified on pole, but his ideal lap still wasn’t as good as Ferrari’s. The chart also shows that they’ve been fairly consistent over the course of the season despite missing out on having the outright fastest pace at all events bar Singapore, making it even more painful that they missed out on their first pole of the year.

Of the top four teams, McLaren have arguably been more up-and-down than the others as they’ve struggled for consistency across different tracks. The MCL40 had its best Qualifying pace when Norris returned to P1 in Hungary and the Netherlands, but it has suffered from a straight-line speed deficiency that somewhat explains the team’s rather sudden decline following the Briton’s Madring success.

The 27 tracks Verstappen has won at after Singapore triumph

The quartet is grouped relatively close together, reflecting the current standings, but the disparity increases as you look down the order. Let’s start with Racing Bulls – they may be ‘best of the rest’ at the moment, but it’s not been a smooth journey for them in Qualifying.

Their high points are clear and include Barcelona, Belgium and Italy, where one of their drivers progressed to Q3. Interestingly, their hard-fought double Q3 appearance in Austria signifies a dip on the chart due to just how dominant the Silver Arrows were, with Russell qualifying on pole by more than two-tenths over everyone else.

As the midfield battle developed, Racing Bulls had a significant downturn in Qualifying pace in Spain and Baku – Alpine did too, but that was anticipated after Pierre Gasly’s surprise success at Monza. There, the Frenchman was perfectly placed amongst the traffic in Q3, allowing him to receive a double slipstream effect on every straight.

Combined with the low downforce conditions that Alpine tend to thrive in, everything fell into place for Gasly to secure his first career pole position. Mercedes still beat them on outright pace, but both of their drivers were caught out by Verstappen’s mistake heading into Turn 1.

Next up are Audi, a team that peaked in Barcelona (where Nico Hulkenberg and Gabriel Bortoleto wound up P9 and P12) and Italy – more proof that Monza was a notable highlight for the midfield, with Haas similarly extracting close to their best Qualifying pace of the season.

But that’s largely where the positives end for the American outfit, unless you go all the way back to Round 2 in China where they had the sixth-best Qualifying pace of anyone and Ollie Bearman squeezed into Q3. Their erratic line on the chart mirrors the “inconsistencies” their drivers have complained of from weekend to weekend, with Monaco, Hungary and Bahrain their worst showings when it comes to a single lap.

Another team that’s failed to see regular improvement is Williams. After a gradual slump in the first half of the year, they plummeted in Hungary – when competitors Aston Martin brought a colossal 16 upgrades – before rediscovering some pace with their own updates in Baku.

Aston Martin’s upgrades were sorely needed, the team having dropped significantly below everyone for five rounds in Europe. They lost some performance once again in Italy, but have generally been on the up since then to get back ahead of Cadillac.

While it might have been comforting for the newcomers to have company at the back of the field, Cadillac have made their own progress too. They originally had a >5% deficit to Mercedes at the season opener and reduced it to under 3% in Belgium, but are still considerably adrift.

Race pace

NB: The Monaco Grand Prix was omitted from the information below as it isn't an ideal event where teams' full pace is exploited.

We’ve been through the Qualifying data, but what about the all-important race pace? It won’t be a shock to see that Mercedes have predominantly been at the top, although not as much as on the previous graph.

That’s because McLaren, Ferrari and Red Bull have all demonstrated that they can beat the leaders in this metric, but haven’t always executed to their full potential. If they had, Mercedes’ win tally would be on nine rather than the 11 they’ve clinched so far.

While that might not sound like the biggest difference, it shows what could’ve been for their rivals. Take McLaren – their highest-scoring round of the season came in Miami, but it was still Antonelli who held on to win the Grand Prix despite McLaren’s superior optimal race pace.

Unlike some of their Qualifying results, Ferrari did capitalise in this regard to secure two victories in Barcelona and Great Britain before falling behind, aligning with Leclerc’s comments about losing ground to the others.

They did, however, bounce back in Singapore and were level with Red Bull’s race pace, indicating just how impressive it was that Verstappen won by 7s over the Monegasque. On that, the Milton Keynes-based outfit have been the fastest team since Round 15 in Azerbaijan, where Verstappen missed out on victory by the smallest of margins.

The only other time they were top was in Austria as they had quicker free air pace than Mercedes after introducing a major upgrade package. Nevertheless, the required pace to overtake was around 0.5s per lap for a 50% chance, so with Verstappen’s advantage lingering around 0.4s, he simply lacked the speed to pass Russell.

Elsewhere, Alpine have been on quite the rollercoaster. They scored points in the first seven rounds despite a decline in their race pace from Japan onwards, which hit a low in Barcelona. From then, Racing Bulls found some crucial performance to edge ahead, so much so that Alpine’s own improvement wasn’t enough to prevent the gap from opening up.

The 2026 Qualifying and race head-to-heads so far

Another notable dip came for almost everyone in the Netherlands thanks to Norris’ immense dominance of the Grand Prix – he beat Mercedes to the chequered flag by 11.536s following McLaren’s aerodynamic-focused upgrades.

Going back to Alpine, they joined the rest of the midfield in improving massively just two weeks later, finishing behind the top teams after Gasly dropped from pole to P7. They also left Singapore with the fifth-best race pace, which should give them some optimism in their fight for P5 in the Constructors’ Championship.

You might expect Racing Bulls to be close considering their 32-point lead over Alpine, but it’s actually Audi that have done the best job in closing the gap. Although all three have been on a similar trajectory, Racing Bulls stagnated in recent events whilst Audi surged forward, reflected in Hulkenberg’s double-score in the Singapore Sprint and Grand Prix.

Haas have recovered to be there or thereabouts too following a big drop that saw them competing against Williams rather than the higher midfield outfits, with recent points-scoring finishes in Baku and Singapore coinciding with their improvement.

On the other hand, the difference in Williams’ pace for each event makes for tough viewing. Up to Round 5 in Canada, they were heading in a great direction that came crashing down in Barcelona; P12 for Carlos Sainz doesn’t sound too bad, but he was two laps down on the winner and ordered the team to “go back to the drawing board” after his dire weekend.

More drastic highs and lows unfolded before their highly-anticipated Baku upgrades, which didn’t deliver enough to seriously reduce their deficit. Instead, their race pace has decreased in the rounds since, which could suggest that the package was too little, too late considering the development of teams around them.

There’s more bad news for Williams too, as they converged with Aston Martin and Cadillac in Singapore, which would be a cause for celebration for the latter two. Aston Martin went down the same path of putting their resources into one big upgrade package, which paid off as they saw a big spike in race pace when it debuted in Hungary.

They haven’t been as consistent as they had likely hoped in the weeks since, but it has largely kept them clear of Cadillac – with the exception of the Azerbaijan Grand Prix. To that end, the American team have made tangible progress, especially after the extreme low in Austria where they failed to log enough laps to determine their race pace.

Car development

As we’ve mentioned, the development push from each team has played a crucial role in influencing the pecking order. Their respective approaches have varied wildly, with some implementing regular changes (like Ferrari and Red Bull) whilst others have depended on a sole boost to move forwards, such as Aston Martin.

But none of them have progressed quite as much as Alpine – they found 1.03s between the Australian and Singapore Grands Prix, trimming their disadvantage to the fastest team from over 1.5s to almost 0.5s.

With Mercedes remaining the reference point, Red Bull are second when it comes to season development, having unlocked 0.62s to nearly equal the Silver Arrows. Ferrari and McLaren have also improved by 0.43s apiece, but while the former are now marginally ahead on the chart, that doesn’t mean that they’re the outright fastest.

It only shows the gaps covered, so the conclusion is that there are now three teams (Mercedes, Ferrari and Red Bull) in close contention on any given weekend. The figures rely on everyone delivering their ideal lap when it matters, which means we can’t state that the Scuderia are definitively quicker, particularly as performance fluctuates depending on the circuit.

Although Aston Martin and Cadillac have also gained 0.50s and 0.37s respectively, they remain at the bottom of the pile behind Williams, who have only recovered 0.18s despite bringing in major upgrades.

Audi are around two-tenths faster than they were at the beginning of 2026, but are still over a second adrift of Mercedes, as are Racing Bulls.

All of that progress makes Haas’ loss of 0.21s even harsher as they’re the only team that have gone backwards. Their strong start to the season may have rapidly faded away, but better results in the last few rounds could give some hope that they can turn things around and hold off Audi for P7.

title: Why Brown thinks Piastri is 'back to the driver I know'
excerpt:
McLaren CEO Zak Brown is feeling confident that Oscar Piastri is back to the driver he knows following a tricky start to the season.

Piastri has faced a challenging 2026 so far, struggling to consistently extract performance from the new generation of cars after finishing third in the Drivers' Championship last season.

The Australian has secured two podium finishes this year, but has found himself unable to match the pace of team mate Lando Norris, who has claimed two Grand Prix victories and outqualified him at 11 of the 17 rounds so far.

However, following that difficult spell Brown believes there are encouraging signs that Piastri is beginning to reclaim his confidence.

Asked in Friday's press conference at the Singapore Grand Prix about whether the 25-year-old was returning to the driver he knew, Brown responded: “I think he is.

“I think we've seen with these cars, it's kind of mixed up the field a little bit, right? Lewis [Hamilton] is getting the better out of the Ferrari right now, George [Russell] got more out of the car last year than Kimi [Antonelli].

“That’s moved around. I think these cars are so complex. Some have adapted a little bit quicker than others, but I’m liking what I’m seeing out of Oscar.

“He’s feeling more confident and on top of things. I like where both our drivers are now.”

Piastri’s difficulties this season have largely centred on adapting his natural driving style to the demands of the MCL40, with McLaren Team Principal Andrea Stella previously explaining that the Australian has been unable to drive through “pure instinct” in certain conditions.

Ahead of the Azerbaijan Grand Prix Piastri acknowledged that finding a solution has been far from straightforward, but praised the team’s efforts to help him improve.

“A lot of the things that have worked for me previously don’t really seem to work this year, so it’s about trying to find different things that do work,” he explained.

“I’m making some progress on that but it’s not as simple as you find one direction and that just works for you all the time. You need to constantly adapt and change things.”

At the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, Piastri finished sixth following a difficult afternoon in Sepang, where a decision to start on medium tyres in wet conditions forced him into an early pit stop.

Despite that result, the nine-time race winner was encouraged by his own performance, although he admitted that McLaren still had work to do to close the gap to their rivals.

How Norris' radio offer supported Stella's team-first ethos

Piastri subsequently finished fifth at the Singapore Grand Prix, although his weekend proved eventful, with the Australian retiring from Saturday’s Sprint following a collision with team mate Norris on the final lap, before a slow puncture on Sunday forced him into an unscheduled pit stop.

Reflecting on that P5 performance, having overtaken Hamilton on the final lap, Piastri said: “It felt pretty reasonable I would say. I think we just didn’t quite have enough pace.

“We couldn’t go with Max [Verstappen] and Charles [Leclerc]. I think Kimi was a little bit quicker than us as well. There wasn’t really too much we could do other than where we ended up.”

With the season progressing into its final stages, Brown remains hopeful that McLaren can build on their recent progress, although he acknowledged the challenge posed by an increasingly competitive field.

“The target is to come into every weekend with the chance to win,” he explained.

“We feel more on top of things than we have for the past couple of races, and we won the last couple of races prior to that.

“It shows how competitive the sport is and how quickly the top four teams, the whole grid for that matter, is moving around in levels of competitiveness.

“Our goal is to try to come to each race weekend and win, but that’s easier said than done.”

title: Ferrari's Larsen to return for 2027 F1 ACADEMY campaign
excerpt:
Ferrari have announced that Alba Larsen will become the first driver to contest a third campaign in F1 ACADEMY, continuing as part of the Scuderia Ferrari Driver Academy next season.

The first driver to land a seat in the all-female series for 2027, the Dane has been granted a third season following a rule change announced last year, which is available exclusively to drivers whose performance indicates strong potential for continued growth.

Larsen was signed by the SFDA midway through her debut F1 ACADEMY season in 2025, achieving 10 top-10 finishes in the Tommy Hilfiger car. Switching to the Ferrari car this year, she recently claimed her first podium in the series, with back-to-back P2 finishes in Zandvoort.

The 17-year-old currently sits fourth in the drivers’ standings with two rounds in Austin and Las Vegas remaining, and also scored her first win in British F4 earlier this season.

"After two years in F1 ACADEMY, I’ve seen first-hand how much this series has grown and how important it’s become," said Larsen.

"Susie [Wolff, F1 ACADEMY Managing Director] and the team keep pushing it forward, the fans bring so much energy, and I’ve had an incredible team around me.

"I’ve grown a lot here too. I’m really proud to be part of it and can’t wait to be back on the grid with Scuderia Ferrari HP in 2027.”

title: The top 10 driver/team combination wins in F1 history
excerpt:
Max Verstappen's victory in the Singapore Grand Prix last weekend was not only his first win at the venue, but also ensured the four-time World Champion moved a step closer to another record.

It was the Dutchman's 73rd victory for Red Bull since he joined the team during the 2016 season, moving him up to second on the list of the most successful driver/team combinations.

But who has more wins with a single team than Verstappen, and who else makes the top 10?

10. Damon Hill/Williams – 21 wins

Following in the footsteps of his father and two-time World Champion, Graham, Damon Hill made his F1 debut with Brabham in 1992, while also acting as test and reserve driver for Williams.

Given a race seat for the 1993 season alongside champion-elect Alain Prost, Hill's maiden win came at the Hungarian Grand Prix after losing likely victories in the previous British and German races due to an engine failure and puncture respectively.

He continued his winning ways, securing a hat-trick of success in Belgium and Italy, and with the death of new team mate Ayrton Senna in the San Marino Grand Prix the following season, proved to be Michael Schumacher's biggest threat for the 1994 title.

Although 10 victories came across the 1994 and 1995 campaigns, it took until the 1996 season for Hill to claim the ultimate prize, clinching the title at the Japanese Grand Prix in what was his final victory for Williams as he left the team.

9. Nico Rosberg/Mercedes – 23 wins

Like Hill, Nico Rosberg also followed in the footsteps of his father and 1982 World Champion, Keke, and made his debut with Williams at the 2006 Bahrain Grand Prix.

Four seasons yielded only two podiums, and for 2010 Rosberg jumped to Mercedes as the Silver Arrows made their return to F1 as a constructor for the first time since 1955.

Rosberg's breakthrough victory came at the 2012 Chinese Grand Prix, before he secured the first of three wins at the Monaco Grand Prix the following season.

With Mercedes the dominant force in F1 under the new-for-2014 regulations, a plethora of wins followed for Rosberg over the next three seasons as he battled team mate Lewis Hamilton for the title.

Nine victories in 2016, including his final F1 win at the Japanese Grand Prix, ensured Rosberg of the title before the German made a shock decision to retire from the sport.

8. Jim Clark/Lotus – 25 wins

Jim Clark spent his entire F1 career driving Colin Chapman's Lotus cars from 1960 until his death in a Formula 2 race at Hockenheim in 1968.

Considered the best driver of his generation and an all-time great in the sport, Clark dominated grand prix racing at the wheel of Chapman's rapid but often fragile machines, usually either winning the race or retiring.

The Scot's first victory came at the 1962 Belgium Grand Prix – a race he won on four consecutive occasions – as two more wins put him on the cusp of the title, only for an oil leak to deny him at the final round in South Africa.

There was no stopping Clark in 1963, as seven wins from 10 races secured a maiden title, a feat he repeated in 1965 with six more victories, as another oil leak denied him a hat-trick of titles on the final lap in the 1964 decider.

Clark's talent ensured he secured at least one F1 victory across seven seasons, as well as the 1965 Indianapolis 500, with his final win coming at the 1968 season-opener in South Africa, just three months before losing his life.

7. Nigel Mansell/Williams – 28 wins

Nigel Mansell amassed 28 wins for Williams across three different spells with the team, ensuring the Briton still holds the most victories for the Grove-based outfit.

After five seasons with Lotus which yielded podiums but no wins – most memorably hitting the barrier at Monaco in 1984 when leading in the rain – Mansell jumped to Williams for 1985 where the breakthrough finally came at the European Grand Prix, held in front of his home fans at Brands Hatch.

Another win immediately followed in South Africa next time out, setting Mansell up to challenge for the 1986 title up until the final round in Adelaide, before a spectacular puncture ended his chances after a season with five wins.

Mansell went even better the following season with six victories, but a heavy crash in Qualifying for the Japanese Grand Prix left him out of the race and ended his chances.

A barren 1988 season meant Mansell moved to Ferrari for two seasons (securing three wins which were the only times he never won with a Williams), before moving back to Williams for 1991.

After pushing Senna close for the title, all the stars finally aligned for Mansell in 1992 as he secured the title with nine victories to his name, including a third and final win at Silverstone, before focusing on racing in America.

Senna's death prompted a part-time return to Williams at several points in 1994, with Mansell securing his final victory in his final race for the team at the season-ending Australian Grand Prix.

6. Alain Prost/McLaren – 30 wins

Alain Prost began his career with McLaren in 1980, but it was with Renault over the following three seasons where he secured his maiden F1 victory and first challenged for the title.

A return to McLaren in 1984 yielded his first win for the team at the season-opener in Brazil, before six further wins brought him to within just half a point of the title, which ultimately went to team mate Niki Lauda.

Back-to-back titles followed as Prost racked up nine wins across the two campaigns, and more top step appearances came in 1987 and 1988 despite not winning the title. The latter season was his first alongside Senna, the duo sharing 15 wins from 16 races (seven for Prost).

The Frenchman claimed his third and final title for McLaren the following season as he and Senna collided together in Japan, with Prost's last win for the team coming at the Italian Grand Prix.

Further wins came with Ferrari and Williams, the latter team where he secured his fourth and final title before retiring at the end of 1993.

5. Ayrton Senna/McLaren – 35 wins

Ayrton Senna is synonymous with McLaren, claiming all three of his titles with the team and 35 of his 41 F1 victories, which still remains the record for the Woking-based squad.

After three seasons and six wins with Lotus, Senna joined McLaren for the 1988 season, taking the first of eight victories at the San Marino Grand Prix en route to his maiden F1 title.

Although six more wins followed the following season, unreliability and a clash with Prost in Japan meant he fell short of back-to-back crowns.

Another collision between himself and Prost the following season in Japan, with the Frenchman now at Ferrari, handed the title in favour of Senna, who had taken six wins during the campaign, before a third and final title came in 1991, which included a first win in front of his home fans in Brazil.

A second win would come in Sao Paulo in 1993, as well as six wins on the streets of Monte Carlo which still stands as a record, as Senna and McLaren ultimately failed to match the dominance of Williams.

Senna's final victory both for McLaren and in F1 came at the 1993 Australian Grand Prix where he was joined on the podium by Prost, whom he replaced at Williams the following season before losing his life after just three races with the team at the San Marino Grand Prix.

4. Sebastian Vettel/Red Bull – 38 wins

After securing a maiden F1 victory against all the odds for midfield team Toro Rosso during a wet 2008 Italian Grand Prix, it was only logical that Sebastian Vettel would be drafted into the senior Red Bull squad for the 2009 season.

In even more torrid conditions, the young German secured Red Bull's first victory as the team also took a 1-2 during the Chinese Grand Prix, before Vettel racked up three further victories as he and the team found their feet.

The 2010 season witnessed one of the closest title battles in F1 history, with Vettel an outside bet for the accolade after four victories that year, but another win in the Abu Dhabi decider and other results gifted him a first unexpected title.

Armed with Adrian Newey's creations that tended to be one step ahead of the opposition, Vettel and Red Bull became an unstoppable force as they secured four titles in succession, with the German amassing 38 wins with the team.

His final victory came at the 2013 Brazilian Grand Prix, but after a winless 2014 campaign, Vettel moved to Ferrari where 14 more wins beckoned.

3. Michael Schumacher/Ferrari – 72 wins

After back-to-back titles with Benetton in 1994 and 1995, Michael Schumacher went in search of a greater challenge and moved to Ferrari, which had yet to win a drivers' title since 1979.

Despite being no match for that year's Williams, it didn't take long for Schumacher's talent to shine through as he won his first race for the Scuderia on just his seventh start, in monsoon conditions at the Spanish Grand Prix.

Two further victories followed before a title tilt in 1997 ended with Schumacher disqualified from the points standings after a clash with Jaques Villeneuve in the final race, although the German kept his five victories.

Further victories came over the following two seasons, but it took until the 2000 campaign for Schumacher to claim his third title and first with Ferrari after a season with nine wins.

It started a run of five drivers' titles on the bounce as Schumacher and Ferrari became the dominant force in F1, only ending in 2005 as new regulations were introduced.

After finding their winning form again in 2006, Schumacher challenged Fernando Alonso for the title and took his final victory for Ferrari and in F1 during a wet 2006 Chinese Grand Prix.

Having missed out on the title and entering retirement at the end of the season, Schumacher returned in 2010 for three seasons with Mercedes, which produced just a single podium.

2. Max Verstappen/Red Bull – 73 wins

Max Verstappen moved another step closer to another record last weekend as he jumped up to second in this list, having finally won on the streets of Singapore.

All of the Dutchman's 73 wins have come with Red Bull, having claimed his first win for the team on his debut at the 2016 Spanish Grand Prix, becoming the youngest F1 race winner at the age of just 18 in the process.

Further sporadic victories came over the following seasons, but it wasn't until 2021 when Red Bull had a car capable of matching Mercedes and Lewis Hamilton. Verstappen claimed 10 victories in one of the all-time great F1 seasons as he and Hamilton went head-to-head, with the Red Bull driver eventually coming out on top.

Three further titles beckoned, including a 2023 campaign which produced a record 19 wins from 22 races, before just missing out on the 2025 title by just two points after a late fightback which included six wins in the final nine races.

Despite having to wait until the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to secure his first win of the 2026 campaign, a second dominant victory followed last weekend in Singapore as Verstappen and Red Bull look like hitting their stride once again.

1. Lewis Hamilton/Mercedes – 84 wins

When Lewis Hamilton announced he would leave McLaren for Mercedes, many were skeptical that such a career move would prove successful as the German manufacturer struggled to find its feet in F1.

But over a 12-year period that began in 2013, Hamilton and Mercedes proved to be the most successful partnership in F1 history, amassing 84 wins and six drivers' titles together.

Hamilton's first win with the team came in his maiden season at the Hungarian Grand Prix, before embarking on a run of six titles between 2014-2020 that was only broken by team mate Nico Rosberg's success in 2016.

Eight wins came in the 2021 season as Hamilton ultimately lost out to Verstappen, before two seasons where the seven-time World Champion went winless.

There was some final success in their final season together, Hamilton claiming a record ninth win in the British Grand Prix, before his final Mercedes win came at the Belgian Grand Prix after on-the-road winner and team mate George Russell was disqualified post-race.

After another surprise move, this time to Ferrari, Hamilton finally secured his first Grand Prix win for the Scuderia in Barcelona earlier this season.

title: 'We see huge potential' – Komatsu on choosing Camara for Haas
excerpt:
"We see huge potential in Rafa," says Haas Team Principal Ayao Komatsu when we chat in a central London hotel on the day the American team announced they had signed Ferrari junior and F2 championship leader Rafael Camara for 2027.

"He's somebody with whom we can grow together – so I'm really excited to make sure that we can maximise his potential."

With Ollie Bearman expected to get a third season with Haas, it'll mean Komatsu's Formula 1 squad will take on the 2027 campaign with a pair of 21-year-olds. For context on how young that is, double World Champion and Aston Martin racer Fernando Alonso is older than the two of them combined.

It's a bold move – but it's one that Komatsu feels confident in for several reasons.

Firstly, the Japanese boss is utterly convinced of the Brazilian rookie's speed. He saw it externally through his title-winning F3 campaign last year and during this season when he's built momentum across the year in F2 on his way to taking the championship lead last time out in Baku.

And he's seen from the inside, when he ran Camara in old-spec Haas machinery during a two-day test in Portimao, Portugal, in August. The 21-year-old's performance in what was essentially a shoot-out with fellow young racers Leo Fornaroli – who won F2 last year and is McLaren's reserve – and the American team’s own reserve driver duo of Jack Doohan and Toyota-backed Ryo Hirawaka, was particularly special.

"It was really incredible the feeling he has got to understand the grip level – and adjust to all the conditions," says Komatsu of that test run. "In cool conditions, he set a pretty impressive lap time. Then the conditions got worse so the car becomes more difficult to drive – but he didn't panic at all.

"He just drove to the conditions. Then there was a four-hour gap and the conditions were different again. He started with a pretty good lap time – and then had two more runs. The rate of improvement was just incredible."

Another element that stood out for Komatsu was the way Camara handled himself. "Everyone has got a different way to handle pressure," says Komatsu. "I think his focus was right. He wasn't focused on the result.

"I always say that we need to focus on what's in our control. Rafa did exactly the same. He thought: 'How can I be the best version of myself?' Then he maximised everything. He understood how to put himself in the mindset to get the best out of himself – so the overall package was impressive."

With the data from that test, Komatsu sat down with team owner Gene Haas to discuss driver options for the second seat to replace Esteban Ocon.

"It was close," said Komatsu. "I feel we were in a very lucky position. All the drivers who were in the frame for the assessment got the best out of themselves and their attitude was second to none. All of them were professional in the way they approached it and the way they managed the pressure was impressive."

Haas sign Ferrari junior Rafael Camara for 2027

Komatsu's confidence in having another young driver

Camara emerged as the frontrunner following his approach both on and off the track and – with owner Gene Haas already having been aware of Camara's ability having followed him in F2 this year – they quickly came to an agreement.

It can be considered a little bit of a risk to take on a rookie, especially as it's set to be alongside a driver who only made his full-time debut in 2025, but Haas have proved they are capable of getting the best out of a youngster.

Bearman arrived at Haas off the back of a stunning super sub performance for Ferrari in Saudi Arabia in 2024 and set about rewarding both Ferrari and Haas' respective belief in him with a string of encouraging performances which peaked with a sensational P4 in Mexico. Haas have got the best out of him – and that has continued into this year, with Bearman outperforming one-time race-winning team mate Ocon.

With that in mind, Komatsu had the confidence to bring in another rookie for 2027, especially one who was so highly-rated by Ferrari and so impressive when testing Haas machinery.

"When we first met Ollie, the potential was clear," says Komatsu. "I was convinced that he is an amazing talent and we got to know each other. I was sure we can make success of it, that we can grow together, we can create a good environment for each other, support each other and then grow.

"That's exactly what happened, what's been happening for us for a year and half, at least in the full-time racing season, but even before that, doing FP1s in the year, before six FP1, we've been growing together. We proved we can do it."

What's next?

Camara's immediate focus will be securing the F2 championship, with two rounds to go in Qatar and Abu Dhabi respectively.

But between now and the end of the year, the 21-year-old will begin his integration into the team. Sources say that will involve a run in FP1 this year – most likely at his home event in Brazil – and some mileage in the end-of-season young driver test in Abu Dhabi.

Haas haven't announced the identity of his team mate yet – but Komatsu confirmed that it is his intention to continue with Bearman after his impressive second campaign.

"It's a matter of time, but it's not fully under my control," said Komatsu. "He's such a great guy to work with. His speed is totally clear. If you saw the race in Singapore, the overtakes that he did were amazing. The conviction he has, the accuracy he has – it's just brilliant.

"He is such a pleasure to watch and pleasure to work with and he's got such a positive personality and he motivates the team well.

"In the middle of the season when the car wasn't performing, everybody was struggling. As a driver, you get frustrated. You could be driving better than last year when he did a P4 in Mexico, but your result is P15 so as a driver you are so frustrated.

"But he has awareness and mindset to then change that very, very quickly to say: ‘Okay how can I motivate this thing, how can I pick everyone up?' That shows his amazing character so our objective is to continue with him next year."

title: How long do the drivers’ current contracts last?
excerpt:
One of the hottest topics during every Formula 1 season is that of drivers’ futures, with some close to their contract expiry date, some signed up for the short-term and others boasting longer deals. So, who will be driving where in 2027 and beyond as things stand?

McLaren

Lando Norris: 2030

Norris is contesting his eighth season in F1, and at McLaren specifically, with both the driver and team staying loyal to each other. In August 2026, he announced a deal that will keep him in papaya until at least the end of 2030 – for what will be by then a monster 12-season stint with the squad.

Oscar Piastri: ‘Multi-year’ deal

Having impressed greatly since his F1 debut in 2023, Piastri has been locked down by McLaren until at least the end of the 2027 season, and possibly longer. As with any contract, there are likely to be various options and clauses on both sides.

Mercedes

George Russell: 2027

Russell has raced for Mercedes since 2022, spending three seasons alongside Lewis Hamilton and 2025 alongside newcomer Kimi Antonelli. After lengthy negotiations with team boss Toto Wolff, the Briton’s latest deal – taking him through at least 2026 – was confirmed last October.

In a media session earlier this season, Russell offered extra detail on his contract situation, saying: “I will be here next year with the team and that's that. There's not really much more to say.

“It's a multi-year deal. It's numerous years, as we said last year, and often in a lot of these contracts, even if metrics aren't hit, if things are happy then you continue, but as I said, metrics will very likely be hit.”

Kimi Antonelli: 2027

Mercedes opted for an unchanged 2026 line-up by also sticking with Italian teenager Antonelli, whose rookie campaign featured a combination of incredible highs and painful lows, as well as persistent off-track noise linking Mercedes to Red Bull’s Verstappen.

It is understood that Antonelli has been retained by Mercedes for a third season and will form an unchanged line-up with Russell in 2027.

Red Bull

Max Verstappen: 2030

Following months of speculation regarding Verstappen's future – with his management known to have held talks with McLaren – he boldly committed to signing a new deal that will see him stay at Red Bull until the end of 2030, building on his previous contract that went through to 2028.

Although the team have lost their control on the field over the last couple of seasons, the extension indicated Verstappen's belief that they will fight for titles in the near future.

Isack Hadjar: 2027

Hadjar earned promotion to Red Bull for the 2026 season after an impressive rookie term at Racing Bulls, and went on to deliver the regular points finishes needed to receive a contract extension for 2027 – despite missing three rounds with a wrist injury.

The French youngster has fully embraced the challenge of going up against the illustrious Verstappen, producing highlights like a podium finish in Monaco and a memorable charge from P21 to P6 in the Belgian Grand Prix.

Ferrari

Charles Leclerc: ‘Multi-year’ deal beyond 2028

Leclerc agreed a new multi-year deal with Ferrari ahead of the 2026 Monaco Grand Prix with sources saying it takes him beyond the end of 2028 with the Scuderia. That keeps him at the team into his 30s and for at least a decade – and it's likely there are mechanisms within the deal to extend his stay beyond that if both sides agree.

Lewis Hamilton: ‘Multi-year’ deal

Hamilton’s blockbuster switch from Mercedes to Ferrari was also communicated under a multi-year headline. There have been suggestions that the deal is for three years, running through 2027, which is the length of contract he pursued at the Silver Arrows.

Williams

Alex Albon: 2027

A former Red Bull racer himself, Albon returned to F1 with Williams in 2022 and has since made the Grove-based outfit his home. The Thai-British racer signed a new deal ahead of the 2026 Dutch Grand Prix that runs until the end of 2027, prolonging his status as the driver to record the most starts for Williams.

Carlos Sainz: ‘Multi-year’ deal

Williams pulled off a coup when they won the race to sign Ferrari’s proven Grand Prix winner Sainz for 2025. The Spaniard has since agreed to a second multi-year contract to help the team fulfil their ambition of fighting at the front once again. It is understood his deal runs until the end of 2028, though there are believed to be clauses within that deal that could allow him to leave earlier.

The announcement was made shortly after Albon's, giving Williams stability as they prepare to head into 2027.

Racing Bulls

Liam Lawson: 2026

Lawson has been rebuilding his F1 career after a rapid-fire Red Bull promotion and demotion last year. He rediscovered some form at Racing Bulls as 2025 developed, becoming a frequent points scorer, and secured another season at the outfit for 2026.

Arvid Lindblad: 2026

Lindblad is the latest Red Bull prospect to reach F1, starting out with a Racing Bulls seat through 2026. The 18-year-old impressed on his debut in Australia by becoming the third-youngest driver in the sport’s history – and the youngest British driver – to score points.

Aston Martin

Fernando Alonso: 2026

At 44, Alonso is the oldest driver on the F1 grid, but the two-time World Champion – who won those titles with Renault in the mid-noughties – is continuing as an Aston Martin driver for at least the 2026 season via the multi-year deal he committed to in early 2024.

Lance Stroll: 2026

Stroll has filled a seat at his father Lawrence’s team for several years, stretching back to 2019 and Aston Martin’s previous Racing Point guise. With the Canadian’s latest contract extension confirmed midway through 2024, he is likely to stay put while his dad is at the reins.

Haas

Esteban Ocon: Leaving at end of 2026

Haas signed an all-new driver pairing for last season, having parted ways with Nico Hulkenberg (on his way to Kick Sauber/Audi) and Kevin Magnussen (embarking on a new career in sportscars). Experienced Grand Prix winner Ocon formed half of that line-up on a multi-year agreement, but it was confirmed in September that the Frenchman will leave the team at the end of the campaign after a two-year stint.

Ollie Bearman: ‘Multi-year’ deal

Bearman announced himself to the F1 paddock with a spectacular stand-in performance for Ferrari at the 2024 Saudi Arabian Grand Prix, one that went a long way to him earning a full-time spot at Ayao Komatsu’s squad for 2025 – again on undisclosed multi-year terms. It is thought that the Briton will continue to race for the team into 2027.

Rafael Camara: ‘Multi-year’ deal

Following the announcement that Ocon will leave Haas at the end of the 2026 season, speculation mounted over who would replace him. It has since been confirmed that F2 racer Rafael Camara will make the step up in 2027, the Brazilian having signed a multi-year deal with the American outfit.

Audi

Nico Hulkenberg: ‘Multi-year’ deal

As mentioned above, Hulkenberg left Haas for Audi’s incoming F1 project in 2025 on a multi-year deal, with options that are believed to give him the chance to race for the German automotive giants into his 40s if the partnership works as planned.

Gabriel Bortoleto: ‘Multi-year’ deal

Hulkenberg has been partnered at Sauber/Audi by Brazilian youngster Bortoleto, a back-to-back winner of the F3 and F2 championships who is also part of Alonso’s management stable. He is signed up to the squad through at least the 2026 season.

Alpine

Pierre Gasly: 2028

Alpine has been Gasly’s home since 2023, when the Frenchman cut his ties with the Red Bull family and started a new F1 chapter. He agreed a fresh multi-year deal last September – one that is due to run until at least the end of the 2028 campaign.

Franco Colapinto: 2027

Former Williams super-sub Colapinto returned to F1 with Alpine in early-2025, stepping up from a reserve role and replacing Jack Doohan. It was not the smoothest of rides for the Argentine thereafter, but he did enough to keep his seat alongside Gasly into 2026.

However, this year he has visibly stepped up his performances, scoring 19 points, and has been rewarded with a contract extension into 2027.

Cadillac

Valtteri Bottas: ‘Multi-year’ deal

Bottas spent 2025 in a back-up role at Mercedes after losing his seat at Kick Sauber, but the 10-time Grand Prix winner sealed a return for 2026 with new team Cadillac – signing a deal that will run until at least the end of 2027.

Sergio Perez: ‘Multi-year’ deal

Cadillac chose two pairs of experienced hands for the start to their F1 journey, with six-time Grand Prix winner Perez – who was dropped by Red Bull at the end of 2024 – also making a comeback on similar terms to Bottas.

title: Camara on the ‘crazy’ achievement of joining Haas in 2027
excerpt:
Rafael Camara has a lot going for him. On track, he's killing it. The reigning F3 champion is currently leading the F2 championship with two rounds to go – and he was sensationally fast in Haas' shoot-out test.

Off track, he compartmentalises the fire and killer instinct needed to extract his racing potential and returns to being a kind, quietly-spoken, genuine 21-year-old.

We meet in a Central London hotel on the day he's announced as a Formula 1 driver. Like all of his soon to be rivals, it's a day that he's been dreaming about his whole life. And unsurprisingly, even though it has been some time since he's been told, it hasn't fully sunk in yet.

"It feels good," he says. "I'm very happy. It's something you've been working your whole life for this moment.

"It's just really crazy to achieve this. I'm just looking forward to start working with the team, to meet everyone in the factory and start as soon as possible."

Brazilian Camara entered the year knowing that if he delivered on his promise, Ferrari – whose junior programme he has been part of since 2021 – would almost certainly find a way to get him on the Formula 1 grid in 2027.

So, he got his head down and focused on trying to hit the ground running in F2 with Invicta Racing and put together a tilt at the title.

At times, a championship charge looked difficult – he was 47 points off the lead at one point – but he never panicked.

"I was just trying to make sure I did everything I could to make sure I would have no regrets this year," he continues. "So obviously I cannot be happier right now."

In a short space of time, he took the championship lead – and found out he would be driving for Haas next year. Alongside his F2 commitments, Ferrari also ploughed on preparing him for his arrival in F1 and that included a private test at the Hungaroring in Hungary in May.

A few months later, he found himself in Haas machinery taking part in an old-fashioned shoot-out test as Haas boss Ayao Komatsu evaluated four young drivers while he contemplated a replacement for Esteban Ocon. It was here that he solidified his chance to step up to F1.

Haas sign Ferrari junior Rafael Camara for 2027

"For sure it was an intense two days," says Camara of the test. "Obviously it was a new track, new team. I went to do the seat fit but obviously I didn't meet everyone, so it was a new environment and for sure it was quite intense.

"You have two days to make sure you are comfortable and you deliver what you need to deliver, and I was just a bit concerned about being a bit tight and not being myself. I just really wanted to make sure I was really enjoying because it was not going to be an opportunity that I would have again."

The Brazilian was able to calm those nerves and enjoy it to the extent that he was delivering lap times, in a range of tricky conditions, that made Komatsu and his engineering team take note. They were particularly impressed at how quickly he was able to extract performance out of the car – and adapt to the different conditions while keeping mistakes to a minimum.

I think I have always been able to extract the most of myself.Rafael Camara, F2 leader and future Haas driver

Those are traits that Camara has shown throughout his junior career. On his F3 debut in Melbourne, Australia, he posted the fastest lap on his second push lap in practice, despite never having driven the track before, and then went on to take pole. To be able to commit to a lap in reasonably unfamiliar machinery on a reasonably unfamiliar track was becoming his bread and butter.

"I think I have always been able to extract the most of myself," he says. "These days were really just trying to apply everything that I learned in the years in my single-seater career. Everything that I knew, it's just about putting it in place and making sure I was doing my job."

Camara has made the most of his opportunities. He admits that he was a "bit scared" when he joined the Ferrari junior programme and that he had to work hard to improve his English to in turn improve the way he communicated with the team.

But he threw himself into the challenge and, as a result, he feels like he was "able to learn a lot" and "to grow up not only as a driver but as a person as well" with Ferrari.

Having seen the likes of Charles Leclerc and Ollie Bearman progress from Ferrari juniors to Formula 1 drivers in recent times was also inspiring because he knew that, if he delivered on expectation, there was a strong chance he would get to follow in their footsteps.

Once Komatsu gave him the good news, he told his parents. "I didn't know how to say it to them so I just said quickly – I'll be driving next year," he says laughing. "My dad, he was more emotional. When he came to hug me, it was just... you cannot hold [the emotion], it just comes out."

When he arrives in Formula 1, he'll have some familiar faces around. He's known fellow Brazilian Gabriel Bortoleto since he was a kid, racing him in go-karts along with Kimi Antonelli, Isack Hadjar and Arvid Lindblad.

Why Haas decided to risk promoting rookie Camara

"I have known Gabi since I was seven," he says. "We raced together in Brazil. Then in Europe he was always in the category above but we've always been together.

"We have been very close friends. To see him going [to F1]... for me it was another motivation to keep working and keep pushing so hopefully it would be two of us there – and it will be next year."

For now, though, Camara is resetting his focus to F2 and the final two rounds of the year. He leads Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov by seven points but if he can fend off the Bulgarian, he'll follow in the footsteps of the likes of Bortoleto, Oscar Piastri, George Russell and Leclerc in winning F3 and F2 back-to-back before ultimately making it into Formula 1.

"The aim is to finish on a high," he says. Once that's done and dusted he can switch his attention to the Haas project, with a run in the end-of-season young driver test planned ahead of an intense winter.

"There's a lot of things we need to speak about and organise," he says. "I'll just be waiting for them to tell me what to do – and I'll be ready."

title: Here's how Kimi Antonelli can win the 2026 F1 title in the United States GP
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli title permutations for United States GP

Kimi Antonelli can be crowned the youngest-ever F1 world champion at this weekend's United States Grand Prix in Austin - and this is how he can shatter Sebastian Vettel's record.

Antonelli heads to Austin with 340 points to his name, 102 clear of George Russell in second and 111 ahead of Lewis Hamilton in third place.

For him to be crowned champion, he must leave Texas with a points lead of 125 over Russell, or Hamilton - which he can only achieve with a race victory.

A race win in the United States would automatically knock Max Verstappen, Charles Leclerc, and Lando Norris out of title contention, leaving Russell and Hamilton as the only drivers who could deny Antonelli the title.

If Antonelli wins in Austin, he will move to 365 points, and a lead of 127 points over Russell and 136 over Hamilton.

To keep the deficit to the Italian under the magic 125-point buffer he requires, Russell would be required to finish in eighth place or higher to keep his title hopes alive. This would reduce the gap to Antonelli to 123 points for a P8 finish.

Should Russell finish exactly ninth, he will be exactly 125 points behind Antonelli, but after his ninth grand prix win of the season, the Italian would win the crown on countback as he would hold nine race wins to a maximum of eight for Russell, who would hold three wins with five races left in the season.

When championship points are tied, the first tie-breaker used is the number of grand prix wins for each driver, meaning Antonelli, with nine wins, could not be passed by Russell.

As for Hamilton, if Antonelli wins and extends his points lead to 136 over the seven-time champion, Hamilton would be required to finish fourth or higher.

A fourth-place finish for Hamilton with an Antonelli win in Austin would have the points gap at 124 with 125 remaining. Should Hamilton finish fifth with an Antonelli win, the gap would be 126 points, handing Antonelli the title.

Should he win the world championship, Antonelli will become the youngest champion in F1 history, beating Vettel's record from 2010 by over three years, and also be the first Italian crowned since Alberto Ascari in 1953, 73 years ago.

To date, only the very first F1 world champion - Giuseppe Farina in 1950 - and Ascari in 1952 and 1953 have won the title for Italy.

title: Liam Lawson addresses possible Red Bull exit as Nikola Tsolov decision looms
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has explained his feelings towards a possible exit from the Red Bull family as the decision over Nikola Tsolov looms.

Lawson is enjoying his best season in F1, and has scored points in 12 of the 17 races thus far, and three Sprints, taking a career-equalling best of fifth in Monaco and the Singapore Sprint, to help guide Racing Bulls to the cusp of finishing fifth in the constructors' standings - the first time the Faenza-squad would have done so in F1 under its various guises.

However, despite his strong performances, Lawson's seat is the one believed to be at risk if Red Bull ultimately decide to promote F2 title contender Tsolov into a race seat, with Arvid Lindblad set for a second season following his impressive rookie campaign.

Should Lawson fall off the grid for 2027, there are no options for an immediate race return, but the driver market is more open for 2028, with the New Zealander addressing the possibility of what would happen if he kept his seat for '27, and then departed for pastures new for the '28 season.

"I don't know if I have to do anything, but I think, for me personally, I mean, for all of us as drivers, our goal is to win," Lawson told media, including RacingNews365, when asked if leaving the Red Bull programme at the end of 2027 made sense, if he retained his seat.

"So for me, my focus is to put myself in a position where I can be winning for one, and if I can go to a team that gives me a better chance to do that, that's obviously what we're what we get to do.

"So the Red Bull specifics of it, I think they've shown many times in the past that sometimes that's not entirely why they make decisions, so it is something that I don't know what's going to happen next year, but for me, it's honestly not really what I'm thinking about now.

"I think that's something that has always been sort of talked about, and obviously you always try to cover your bases. But right now, not too much. It's not something that I would say I'm thinking about too much.

title: Oscar Piastri declares 'Mercedes envy' as tricky F1 challenge explained
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri has described how McLaren feels "envy" towards Mercedes with its pace through corners in F1, as he addressed a tricky challenge facing drivers.

Mercedes' W17 machine has been the class of the field in 2026, with 11 wins from 17 races, and is closing in on winning the team a ninth constructors' crown, with Kimi Antonelli on the verge of winning the drivers' championship.

In contrast, McLaren, the reigning constructors' champions, have slipped back in the first year of the new technical regulations and are in a fight for third place with a resurgent Red Bull with the MCL40 machine being tricky to extract performance from.

One aspect of this is the higher tyre pressures which have been mandated by Pirelli as a safety factor in case of straight-line mode failure. With the cars designed around reduced downforce on a straight with active aero open, any failure could place undue stress on the tyres and cause failures.

The higher pressures mean the tyres are prone to 'ballooning' and cannot give drivers the feeling they require to extract maximum performance.

However, Piastri does not believe this is the only reason to explain McLaren's deficit to Mercedes - whom he described as "envying" through the corners.

"If I knew, I'd be a much happier person," Piastri began to media, including RacingNews365, when asked if the tyres were affecting the performance levels in 2026.

"I think in Baku it wasn't a huge surprise to see Mercedes so far ahead, they've been very, very quick everywhere. I think their straight-line speed has always been very strong, and I think the confidence they have on the way into corners is generally something we envy.

"Putting it bluntly, I think some of the laps that Lando's done in qualifying to put the car on pole have been better than what the car deserves, but I think definitely for us, and I can't speak for others, but definitely, if you can break that barrier of what holds you back, you find a lot of lap time, and you know that's kind of the thing.

"Either you're quite a way off, or you're really fast. There's not really an in-between, and that's been a bit of a struggle this year. So I don't think it's necessarily down to the tyres. I

"I think for us there are definitely a few things in how we need to drive the car that are maybe compounding that.

"But even last year we were having stints or weekends where our pace was unbelievable, and we didn't really know why, and we struggled more on other weekends, and we didn't really know why.

"So there are always unknowns, but I don't think it's as simple as just the tyres are very sensitive."

title: F1 warned of 'system stress' and 'fatigue' following recent technical glitches
excerpt:
Martin Brundle believes F1 is showing signs of "fatigue" after recent technical glitches over the last two grands prix weekends in Malaysia and Singapore.

For last Sunday's Bahrain Grand Prix at the Sepang International Circuit, a software patch had to be issued to the teams due to a wet-weather power unit mapping bug causing cars to suffer unrecoverable power loss on the formation lap under the mandatory 250kW restriction.

The FIA distributed an emergency fix that bypassed the restrictive energy limits so cars could safely get going, and has since confirmed a permanent update to the standard ECU's wet-weather parameters will be rolled out for the United States Grand Prix in Austin.

On Friday in Singapore, further confusion arose. Timing screens failed to register multiple drivers' lap times at the end of SQ1, delaying the start of SQ2 by almost 20 minutes while race control verified the classification.

Race control also conceded to an operational "human error" following a crash involving Cadillac's Sergio Perez, briefly activating overtake mode for roughly 27 seconds before it was switched off again, handing an uneven energy boost to only part of the field.

Brundle, speaking on Sky Sports F1, feels the recent technical issues are a sign F1's 'system' is being stressed.

"They fixed it quite quickly," said Brundle, referring to what occurred in Malaysia. "One team needed longer than the others to get it signed off at HQ. That cost another 10 minutes. I won't name that team.

"But there was clearly a problem, in a zone we weren't expecting, on a particular sector of the lap. It was wrong. It shouldn't be, but it was.

"They found a solution, made a patch, the teams put it on their cars, and we all went racing.

"I tell you what I think I'm seeing is fatigue. We've got six races in seven weekends, nine in 11. We parachute into temporary facilities like this [Singapore], random bits of concrete and asphalt around the world.

"We had some more glitches in [sprint] qualifying yesterday, not just from the FIA, that were a bit curious with onboard and driver trackers and lap times, sector times, teleprint, and that sort of thing.

"I think we're just stressing the system a little bit, but it shouldn't happen in the world of Formula 1."

Brundle, though, was clear that his affection for the sport remained undimmed despite the recent run of problems.

"I love driving them [the cars]," he said. "If we had a normally aspirated engine and a gear lever linkage and a throttle cable, we wouldn't be here today with all of this amazing world of Formula 1, maybe hobby racing in Europe."

title: Ferocious F1 progress is invaluable to the wider automotive industry
excerpt:
F1 is the pinnacle of motorsport and the world's fastest laboratory. As a brake manufacturer partnered with every team on the grid, Brembo applies the technology developed here across all other fields, whether in racing or road cars. But how?

18 October 4:30PM

F1 not only provides its technical partners and suppliers with unparalleled visibility and marketing value, but also offers an unmatched opportunity for technological advancement.

Brembo, the brake manufacturer that works with all teams, is a perfect example of how widely F1-perfected technology can be used.

The various technologies, innovations, and achievements stemming from the Italian company's involvement are transferred into other segments of motorsport and everyday road cars.

“Formula 1 is the most challenging championship that we supply, where the technology basically is pushed further every year,” explained Andrea Algeri, racing car market manager of the Italian company in an exclusive conversation with RacingNews365.

“The teams are very fast in trying to push the development, do things even by themselves, and we have to follow them”

[Article continues below]

Technology transfer

Brembo’s technology and expertise are used in numerous racing series, allowing teams in WEC, GT, WRC, Formula E, and MotoGP, among others, to benefit from the work done in the F1 laboratory.

This technology transfer is extensive, even though every racing series has its own unique characteristics.

"For example, in WEC, the components are very close to F1, even if they are not so customised,” said Algeri.

"The solutions are more driven by Brembo compared to F1, where the teams are asking for minimal differences and a lot of customisation of the components.

"The carbon material and the calliper technology are very similar. The brake-by-wire, for example, is even more complicated than F1 because the rules allow you to be more complicated in the sense that the component is more integrated in the car."

Algeri also provided insight into how technology gained in F1 makes its way into the world of road cars. According to the Italian engineer, this transfer comes with its own challenges due to the unique nature of motorsport.

"When the product is good for F1, but you translate it directly without any change on the road car, you still have some problems," he said.

"For example, carbon material needs some temperature to operate and give you the best performance.

"Road car applications need to work at ambient temperature because you are on a highway; you run for several miles without touching the brakes, and then you hit the brakes, and you don't have temperature in this carbon material, so the performance could not be the best.

"However, some modifications in the process allow you to use a similar material with an everyday driver or everyday car with the best performance for that particular application."

[Article continues below]

From F1 to the road cars - and back?

The complications of the technology transfer from racing to public roads obviously require time. Algeri pointed out that this depends entirely on the type of solutions being transferred.

"It could be very fast, but depending on the customer you have, the horizon is at least three to four years," he said.

"This is, I would say, the minimum amount of time that you need to translate one component that is developed in F1 to the standard road car.

"Obviously, it really depends on the example, but even maybe some geometry on the calliper, for example, can be translated quite quickly into a final product. If we talk about carbon materials, it may take even 10 years."

Algeri additionally explained that because the solutions used in F1 are heavily restricted by strict demands and regulations, some road cars today feature brake systems that are technologically more advanced than those in F1 cars.

The explanation is simple: in the world of road cars, engineers are not bound by rigid rules. The brake expert also pointed out that, from time to time, motorsport actually draws inspiration from solutions applied in road cars.

"In some ways, road car applications are now sometimes even more technologically advanced compared to F1," he said. “Why? Because in F1, some areas are limited by the rules."

title: Former Mercedes driver 'confirms' Ferrari F1 test after switch
excerpt:
Ferrari recently signed a new simulator driver, who is set for an F1 test in 2027 with the Scuderia.

Sacha Fenestraz has revealed he will get behind the wheel of a Ferrari Formula 1 car next year as part of a Testing of Previous Cars outing, following his move to Maranello earlier this year.

The French-Argentine driver joined Ferrari as a simulator and development driver in July, having spent three seasons in a similar role with Mercedes at Brackley before switching teams during the summer.

Fenestraz, who has built a career across Super Formula, Super GT and Formula E alongside his simulator duties, described the move to Ferrari as a significant step up in profile.

Speaking to Grande Premio, he said the role closely mirrors what he was doing at Mercedes, with one notable upgrade.

"The truth is, it's a dream to be able to work there, and it's a dream to be with such a big name in motorsport," said Fenestraz.

"The work is great; it's a bit like what I did with Mercedes in Brackley, only now I get to eat some good pasta in Italy and drive a Formula 1 Ferrari in the simulator, and potentially a couple of tests next year as well, so it's a really great opportunity."

Fenestraz explains importance of Ferrari F1 test

Fenestraz went further, confirming that a TPC run in a Ferrari has already been agreed for 2027, even if the exact timing is still being worked out.

TPC running allows teams to use machinery built to older technical regulations for private track sessions outside championship events, giving simulator drivers like Fenestraz valuable seat time without touching current-specification development parts.

Ferrari has yet to confirm publicly whether that outing will fall under TPC rules or come as part of a dedicated rookie test.

"I'm going to have a test next year, I already know that and they confirmed it," the 26-year-old revealed on Singapore race week.

"I was supposed to be there next week, but I can't make it because I have the Super GT race at Autopolis, so oh well, it'll happen eventually.

"I'm really looking forward to it, but obviously the most important thing for them is for me to get in the car to improve my simulator performance.

"All the simulator drivers have to get behind the wheel of a TPC car to gain experience in a Formula 1 car, so I'll just have to wait for that day."

title: Lando Norris makes frank assessment after 'unnecessary' concession
excerpt:
Lando Norris has addressed his failed attempt to overtake Lewis Hamilton in the Singapore Grand Prix, which allowed Kimi Antonelli through, whilst also alluding to his ill-fated move on Oscar Piastri in the sprint.

Lando Norris has admitted he "should have done a better job" battling Lewis Hamilton for third place in the closing stages of the Singapore Grand Prix.

The move cost Norris a shot at the podium and opened the door for Kimi Antonelli, who cruised past the McLaren.

The reigning F1 drivers' champion was running third behind Hamilton at the Marina Bay Street Circuit when he attempted to pass the Ferrari driver into Turn 1 on lap 54.

Both cars ran deep, with the Ferrari taking to the run-off area and Norris losing momentum through the corner. Antonelli pounced immediately, surging past on the exit of Turn 3 and never looking back.

The Mercedes driver, on fresher tyres than both Norris and Hamilton, set off after the Ferrari and quickly claimed the position too, with the stewards later confirming no further action was needed regarding Hamilton's off-track excursion, which had initially been noted, as Norris also managed to overtake the following lap.

Norris, who finished fourth, had no answer for Antonelli's pace once the net had been drawn.

"I should have done a better job battling with Lewis," he said to Sky Sports F1 after the 62-lap race. "It was inevitable that I would have passed him at some point; I just didn't need to try to overtake him where I did.

"I braked a bit late and could have still put a good move in, and he would have had to let me pass because he braked way too late."

[Article continues below]

A weekend of costly calls

The Turn 1 mistake was not the only questionable decision in Norris's weekend.

On the final lap of the sprint, the Briton lunged down the inside of Oscar Piastri into Turn 5 on a damp track, making contact with his team-mate's right-rear tyre as the gap narrowed and Norris caught the inside kerb.

The stewards investigated but took no further action, ruling that both McLaren drivers had contributed to the incident.

Norris later apologised to the team, and the collision prompted McLaren management to hold internal discussions with both drivers, stressing the championship's priority over individual scraps.

It cost the Woking-based squad eight valuable points, and leaves Red Bull just seven points adrift in the fight for third in the constructors' championship.

Reflecting further on the Hamilton attempt into Turn 1, Norris alluded to the incident in the sprint.

"But it was just a bit unnecessary for me, so just not a good weekend for me in terms of making decisions like that," he said.
